title: Judging a position: the four elements

bank.prompt: A rook and six pawns each, on the same files. Who stands better, and on which count?
options: Black, on the piece count: he has a knight and White has no minor piece at all.
White, because his rook is the more active of the two.
Level, because both sides have a rook and the same number of pawns.
bank.reason: Black has an extra knight and nothing else differs — same pawn files, same rook, both kings behind three pawns.

bank.prompt: Tap the one piece on the board that has no opposite number.
bank.reason: The knight on c6. White has no minor piece, so it is the whole difference between the two sides.

bank.prompt: A queen, a rook and five pawns each, Black to move. Who stands better, and why?
options: White, because his pawns control more of the centre.
Black, because White has no pawns left in front of his king and Black still has all three.
Level, because the material is exactly equal.
bank.reason: The count really is level. f2, g2 and h2 are bare while f7, g7 and h7 are intact, and the queens are still on.

bank.prompt: Tap the three empty squares in front of White’s king where his pawns ought to be.
bank.reason: f2, g2 and h2. Black’s king still has all three of its own, which is the entire difference here.

bank.prompt: Four pawns each and nothing but kings. Who stands better, and why?
options: Black, because his pawns sit in two touching pairs and every white pawn stands alone.
White, because his king is nearer the centre.
Level, because four pawns against four with no pieces is a draw.
bank.reason: White’s f-pawns are stacked and none of his four has a neighbour. Black’s a7 and b7 defend each other, as do g7 and h7.

bank.prompt: Tap every white pawn that has no friendly pawn on a next-door file.
bank.reason: All four. The b, e and g files are empty, so a2, h2 and both f-pawns stand alone — and the f-pawns are doubled as well.

bank.prompt: Two rooks against a rook and a bishop, five pawns each. Who stands better?
options: Level, because a rook and a bishop are worth about the same as two rooks.
Black, because the bishop is worth more than a rook in an open position.
White, by about two points: a rook is worth five and a bishop three.
bank.reason: Rook for bishop is the exchange, and it is worth roughly two pawns. Same pawn count on both sides, so nothing offsets it.

bank.prompt: Tap the black piece that White’s extra rook is worth more than.
bank.reason: The bishop on b7. Five against three is the gap, and that is what being up the exchange means.

bank.prompt: Queen, two rooks, a bishop and six pawns each. Who stands better, and why?
options: White, because the black king is stuck on e8 and cannot castle.
Black, because his extra central pawn gives him more space.
Level, because every piece has an exact opposite number.
bank.reason: The material is identical. One king is castled and the other is sitting in the middle with its rooks unable to reach each other.

bank.prompt: Tap both black rooks — the two pieces that still cannot reach one another.
bank.reason: a8 and h8, with the king and a bishop still stranded between them. Rooks only start working once the king is out of the way.

bank.prompt: Four pawns each, kings in the middle. Who stands better, and why?
options: Level, with four pawns each and no pieces on the board.
Black, because his three kingside pawns outnumber White’s two.
White, because his a-pawn is passed and it is far away from both kings.
bank.reason: No black pawn stands on the a or b file, so a3 has a clear run. A passer on the far wing pulls the enemy king away from everything else.

bank.prompt: Tap the white pawn with no black pawn left in front of it or beside it.
bank.reason: The a-pawn. Black has nothing on the a or b file, so nothing can stop it or challenge it on the way.

bank.prompt: Tap the white piece that cannot move to a single square.
bank.reason: The bishop on f1. Its only two squares are e2 and g2, and White has a pawn standing on each of them.

bank.prompt: A minor piece and six pawns each, Black to move. Who stands better, and why?
options: Black, because his knight has squares everywhere and the white bishop has none.
White, because a bishop is worth more than a knight.
Level, because both are minor pieces worth three points each.
bank.reason: Three points each on the chart. On the board one of them moves and the other cannot, and that decides it.

bank.prompt: Tap the two white pawns that are taking every square away from the bishop on f1.
bank.reason: e2 and g2. A bishop on f1 has nowhere else to go, so its own pawns have shut it in completely.

bank.prompt: Tap the black piece that has no legal move at all.
bank.reason: The bishop on a8. Its own pawn on b7 is the only square it could use, so it is walled into the corner.

bank.prompt: A rook, a minor piece and six pawns each. Who stands better, and why?
options: Level, because the pieces match one for one.
Black, because a bishop is the better piece in an endgame.
White, because his knight sits on a strong square and the black bishop has none at all.
bank.reason: No black pawn can ever attack the knight on c5, and the bishop on a8 cannot move. Both pieces are worth three and only one of them counts.

bank.prompt: What would have to change before the bishop on a8 became a real piece again?
options: The pawn on b7 would have to move out of its way.
It would need to be exchanged for the knight on c5.
Nothing. It already covers the long diagonal from the corner.
bank.reason: b7 is the single square the bishop can use, so until that pawn moves the bishop is a spectator. It covers nothing from a8.

bank.prompt: Tap the white piece that has no legal move at all.
bank.reason: The knight on h1. From the corner it can only reach f2 and g3, and White has a pawn on both.

bank.prompt: Tap the two white pawns that are taking every square away from the knight in the corner.
bank.reason: f2 and g3, the only two squares a knight on h1 has. Until one of them moves the knight is stuck there.

bank.prompt: Tap the rook that has already reached the rank where the enemy pawns are sitting.
bank.reason: The black rook on b2. White’s rook is still on the back rank with nothing in front of it to attack.

bank.prompt: Tap every white pawn the rook on b2 actually attacks right now.
bank.reason: Only a2 and c2. A rook stops at the first man it meets on each side, so e2, g2 and h2 are out of reach for now.

bank.prompt: Tap every black pawn the rook on e7 actually attacks right now.
bank.reason: b7 and f7 only. Going left the rook stops at b7 and going right it stops at f7, so a7, g7 and h7 are untouched.

bank.prompt: Tap the white piece that has reached the rank Black’s pawns are standing on.
bank.reason: The rook on e7. Pawns on their starting rank cannot run away from a rook behind them, which is what makes the seventh worth having.

bank.prompt: Black to move. Tap the white piece that is attacked and has nothing defending it.
bank.reason: The bishop on d4. The knight on c6 attacks it and no white man covers the square, so it is simply hanging.

bank.prompt: Black plays Nxd4. Why is that better than it first looks?
options: It opens the c-file for Black’s pieces.
Nothing takes back, so it is a whole bishop rather than a swap.
It forces White to recapture with the knight and ruin his pawns.
bank.reason: Count the takers before you call it a swap. Nothing white covers d4, so Black keeps the bishop and gives nothing.

bank.prompt: What is the first thing to check before calling any capture an even swap?
options: Whether the two pieces are worth the same number of points.
Whether the capture comes with check.
Whether anything can actually take back, and how many times.
bank.reason: Points only matter once you know a recapture is coming. If nothing takes back it is not a swap at all, whatever the pieces are worth.

bank.prompt: You are a pawn up with two queenside pawns against one. Simplify into the ending.
bank.reason: Rxc8 Kxc8 and the rooks are gone. Two pawns against one makes a passed pawn, and with no pieces left nothing blockades it.

bank.prompt: You are a pawn up and nothing else is unbalanced. Which swaps suit you?
options: Swap pieces and keep pawns on, so the extra pawn becomes a bigger share of what is left.
Swap pawns and keep the pieces on, so you still have something to attack with.
Avoid every swap: an extra pawn is too fragile to risk simplifying.
bank.reason: One pawn among many barely shows. One pawn in a king-and-pawn ending is usually the game, so the side ahead heads for the ending.

bank.prompt: Tap the two white pawns that will outnumber Black on that side of the board once the rooks come off.
bank.reason: a2 and b2 against a7 alone. Two against one makes a passed pawn by force, which is why the swap is worth making.

bank.prompt: Black to move. Tap the white piece that cannot move to a single square.
bank.reason: The bishop on c1. Its only squares are b2 and d2 and White has a pawn on each, so it has no legal move.

bank.prompt: Black’s knight on d3 is his best piece. Why would Nxc1 be a mistake?
options: It loses a piece, because nothing is defending the bishop on c1.
It gives up Black’s strongest piece for White’s most useless one.
It allows White to recapture and open the a-file for his rook.
bank.reason: The rook on a1 takes back, so nothing is won. Black hands over the knight that dominates the position for a bishop that could not move.

bank.prompt: Tap the two white pawns that leave the bishop on c1 with nowhere to go.
bank.reason: b2 and d2. Those are the only squares a bishop on c1 can reach, so White has shut his own piece in.

bank.prompt: Tap the black piece that has no legal move at all.
bank.reason: The bishop on f8. Its own pawns on e7 and g7 sit on the only two squares it could use.

bank.prompt: Tap the two black pawns that are taking every square away from the bishop on f8.
bank.reason: e7 and g7. Move either of them and the bishop is a piece again; leave them and it is furniture.

bank.prompt: Black to move. Tap the black piece that has more white men attacking it than black men defending it.
bank.reason: The knight on d4. Three white men hit it — c3, e3 and f3 — and only two hold it, b6 and e5. One attacker too many.
